key_terms.meaning: A finite, non-empty set of symbols, for example Σ = {a, b}.
A finite sequence of symbols drawn from an alphabet, such as abba; written w.
The string with no symbols; its length is 0 and εw = wε = w for every string w.
The set of all strings over Σ, including ε, formed by taking 0 or more symbols.
Σ⁺ = Σ* − {ε}: all strings over Σ of length 1 or more.
Any set of strings over an alphabet; a language L satisfies L ⊆ Σ*.
u is a prefix of w if w = uv; suffix if w = vu; substring if w = xuy for some x, y.
Given a language L and a string w, decide whether w ∈ L; an automaton answers it by running on w.
A 5-tuple M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) with exactly one move per state–symbol pair.
δ̂(q, w) is the state reached from q after reading the whole string w; δ̂(q, ε) = q.
A machine whose transition relation allows zero, one or many next states for one state–symbol pair.
ε-closure(q) is q plus every state reachable from q using only ε-transitions.
The conversion of an NFA to a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states.
p and q are distinguishable if some string w gives exactly one of δ̂(p, w), δ̂(q, w) in F.
A round-based procedure that marks every distinguishable pair of DFA states; unmarked pairs are merged.
A finite automaton whose output depends only on the current state, printed as the state is entered.
A finite automaton whose output depends on the current state and the input symbol, printed on the transition.
A finite automaton whose read head may move left, right or stay, yet it still accepts only regular languages.

takeaways: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols, a string is a finite sequence of them, and a language is just a set of strings.
A DFA keeps exactly one state, which is all the memory it needs about the past to decide the future.
Acceptance is defined with the extended transition function: w ∈ L(M) exactly when δ̂(q₀, w) ∈ F.
An NFA is a convenient way to write a pattern; its many runs are all simulated at once by the subset construction.
ε-transitions add no accepting power, because ε-closures can be computed and the ε-NFA converted to a DFA.
Two states are equivalent when no string tells them apart, and the table-filling algorithm finds every distinguishable pair.
A Moore machine prints on entering a state, a Mealy machine prints on taking a transition, and each can be converted to the other.
A two-way head looks more powerful but still recognises only regular languages.
Every question in this unit is a variation of one question: does this finite-memory machine accept this string?
bank_note: Long answers here ask for a formal definition plus a worked construction (a DFA, a subset-construction table, or a filled minimization table), so always show the tuple, the table and the accepting argument.

bank.q: Define alphabet, string and language. Explain the Kleene star and Kleene plus with an example, and define prefix, suffix and substring.
outline: Σ is a finite non-empty set of symbols; a string is a finite sequence over Σ
Σ* includes ε, Σ⁺ = Σ* − {ε}
A language is any subset of Σ*
Definitions of prefix, suffix, substring with the w = xuy form
One worked example over Σ = {a, b}

bank.q: Give the formal definition of a deterministic finite automaton and explain each component. Draw the transition diagram and transition table for a small example, and state its language.
outline: M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) with every symbol defined
δ : Q × Σ → Q, exactly one move per pair
Diagram: circles for states, double circle for final, labelled arrows
Table: rows are states, columns are symbols
Acceptance via δ̂ and the language L(M) = {w : δ̂(q₀, w) ∈ F}

bank.q: Define the extended transition function δ̂ for a DFA, give its recursive definition, and use it to define the language accepted by the machine.
outline: Base case δ̂(q, ε) = q
Inductive step δ̂(q, wa) = δ(δ̂(q, w), a)
L(M) = {w ∈ Σ* : δ̂(q₀, w) ∈ F}
Worked trace of one string through δ̂
Note that δ̂ is defined by recursion on the length of the string

bank.q: Define a nondeterministic finite automaton. Explain how it differs from a DFA and how acceptance is defined when several runs exist.
outline: NFA as a 5-tuple with δ : Q × Σ → 2^Q
Zero, one or many next states per pair
A run is a sequence of states; w is accepted if at least one run ends in F
DFA is the special case where every δ value is a single state
Compare with a small example showing both an accepting and a rejecting run

bank.q: Explain Moore and Mealy machines with formal definitions, one example each, and state the difference in when the output is produced.
outline: Moore: output λ(q) depends on state only; output string length = input length + 1
Mealy: output λ(q, a) depends on state and symbol; output length = input length
Transition tables for both with an output column
One conversion example
Note that both are finite-state transducers

bank.q: Design a DFA over Σ = {0, 1} that accepts strings containing an even number of 0s and an odd number of 1s. Give the transition table, the diagram and a trace for one accepted and one rejected string.
outline: Four states for the four parity combinations
Start state (even, even); final state (even, odd)
Complete transition table, every entry defined
Trace using δ̂ for e.g. 011 and 010
Argue correctness by the parity invariant

bank.q: Convert the given NFA (or ε-NFA) into an equivalent DFA using the subset construction. Show the state sets, the transition table and the final states.
outline: Start state is the ε-closure of the NFA start state
For each set and symbol compute the union of moves, then take ε-closure
Build the table until no new sets appear
A DFA state is final if it contains any NFA final state
Justify termination: at most 2^n subsets

bank.q: Minimize the given DFA using the table-filling algorithm. Show the marking rounds, the equivalence classes, and the final minimal DFA.
outline: Remove unreachable states first
Mark all pairs with one final and one non-final state
Repeat: mark (p, q) if some symbol a gives a marked pair (δ(p,a), δ(q,a))
Stop when a round adds no marks; unmarked pairs are equivalent
Merge classes and redraw the minimal machine

bank.q: Design a DFA over Σ = {a, b} for all strings ending in ab, and a DFA for all strings whose length is a multiple of 3. Verify membership of a sample string using δ̂ in each case.
outline: Three-state chain for the suffix ab pattern
Modulo-3 counter with states 0, 1, 2 and only state 0 final
Transition tables for both machines
Membership test by computing δ̂ from the start state
Careful handling of strings shorter than the pattern

bank.q: Prove that every language accepted by an NFA is also accepted by a DFA. Explain why the subset construction terminates and what its worst-case state count is.
outline: Define the DFA state as a set of NFA states
Show by induction on the string length that the DFA set equals the set of all NFA states reachable
Final states: those sets intersecting F
Termination because Q has 2^n subsets
State the 2^n upper bound and note it is often loose

bank.q: Show that ε-transitions do not increase the power of finite automata. Describe how to eliminate them and why the resulting machine accepts the same language.
outline: Define ε-closure recursively and show it can be computed for every state
New δ'(q, a) = ε-closure of the union of moves on a from ε-closure(q)
Start state replaced by its ε-closure; final states that reach a final state by ε are marked final
Induction on string length proves the languages equal
Conclusion: ε-NFA, NFA and DFA all define the same class

bank.q: Define equivalent and distinguishable states. Prove that the table-filling algorithm marks exactly the distinguishable pairs, and relate this to the Myhill-Nerode relation.
outline: Distinguishable: a string w sends exactly one of the two to F
Base marking for final versus non-final
Inductive step matches the algorithm's rounds
Soundness and completeness argument
Unmarked pairs are the Myhill-Nerode classes; the minimal DFA is unique up to renaming

bank.q: A two-way finite automaton may move its head left as well as right. Explain why it still accepts only regular languages, and outline a simulation by an ordinary DFA.
outline: Define the machine and its left, right, stay moves
The head may cross a boundary many times, so a naive state-set is not enough
Track the set of states in which the machine can re-enter the unread suffix from the left
That set is finite, giving a DFA over the same alphabet
Conclude: two-way head adds no accepting power

bank.q: Compare DFAs, NFAs and ε-NFAs as models of computation. State the equivalence results and explain what 'equivalence' means here.
outline: All three accept exactly the regular languages
Definitions side by side, one transition function each
Conversions: ε-NFA → NFA → DFA
Equivalence means equal language, not equal structure or state count
Practical value: NFAs are easier to write, DFAs are easier to run

glossary.def: A single object belonging to an alphabet, such as the character a.
A finite non-empty set of symbols, usually written Σ.
A finite sequence of symbols from some alphabet.
The number of symbols in the string, written |w|.
The unique string of length 0, written ε or λ.
The string uv formed by writing the symbols of v after those of u.
Σ*, the set of all strings over Σ including ε.
Σ⁺, the set of all non-empty strings over Σ.
A set of strings over some alphabet; equivalently a subset of Σ*.
Σ* − L, all strings over the alphabet that are not in L.
A five-part machine with one next state for every state and input symbol.
The rule δ giving the next state (DFA) or set of next states (NFA).
δ̂(q, w), the state reached after reading the whole string w from q.
A snapshot of a machine during a run, here simply its current state.
A language accepted by some finite automaton.
A finite automaton whose transition rule may give several next states.
A move that changes state without consuming an input symbol.
The set of states reachable from a state using only ε-transitions, including the state itself.
The method that turns an NFA into a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states.
Two states for which some string leads exactly one of them to a final state.
Two states that no string can tell apart; they can be merged.
The DFA for a language with the fewest states, unique up to renaming of states.
A state-output machine whose output at each step depends only on the state entered.
A transition-output machine whose output depends on the current state and the input symbol.
A finite automaton whose head may also move left and re-read earlier input.
